text.p: The Supreme Court's decision on Thursday to strike down the Communications Decency Act represents the culmination of two years of sparring.
Following is a chronology:
March 1995 - Senator Jim Exon (D-Nebraska) introduces legislation that would criminalize online publication of any material deemed "obscene, lewd, lascivious, filthy, or indecent."

Embedded within a broad and popular telecommunications reform package, the measure emerges from the Senate Commerce Committee emblazoned with a moniker that will soon galvanize Internet users across the globe: The Communications Decency Act.
In response to the legislation, the Electronic Privacy Information Center's David Banisar tells The Washington Post: "Welcome to Digital Singapore."
June 14, 1995 - The Senate passes the CDA, 84-16.
June 22, 1995 - House Speaker Newt Gingrich denounces the Senate bill: "It is clearly a violation of free speech and it's a violation of the rights of adults to communicate with each other."
Aug. 4, 1995 - The House of Representatives passes, 420-4, its Telecommunications Reform Bill, which carries Internet content provisions that make it little more than a replica of Exon's Senate bill.
Dec. 6, 1995 - Joint House/Senate Committee approves final bill for joint House and Senate vote.
Feb 1, 1996 - The House (414-16) and Senate (91-5) vote to approve the Telecommunications Act of 1996, including the CDA.

Feb. 8, 1996 - President Clinton signs the Telecommunications Act. Within minutes of the signing, a coalition led by the American Civil Liberties Union files suit in the U.S. District Court in Philadelphia challenging the constitutionality of the new law.

In a separate suit, Joe Shea, editor of the online newspaper The American Reporter challenges the CDA in Brooklyn, N.Y., federal court, arguing that the "indecency" provisions place an "unfair burden" on online publishers.
Internet users respond with the Great Web Blackout, darkening hundreds of screens across the World Wide Web in the largest organized protest in Internet history.

Feb. 16, 1996 - U.S. District Court Judge Ronald L. Buckwalter of Philadelphia issues an order temporarily blocking enforcement of the CDA. The judge rules that the CDA provision pertaining to "indecent materials" is unconstitutionally vague and would "leave reasonable people perplexed in evaluating what is or what is not prohibited in this statute."

Feb. 26, 1996 - Led by the American Library Association, a coalition of corporations and organizations -- including America Online, the Society of Professional Journalists, the Citizens' Internet Empowerment Coalition, and Wired Ventures -- files a second suit challenging the CDA in U.S. District Court in Philadelphia. The new suit is consolidated with the earlier ACLU suit.
March 21, 1996 - A panel of federal court judges convenes in Philadelphia to hear ACLU v. Reno.

June 12, 1996 - Panel declares CDA unconstitutional. From Judge Stewart Dalzell's opinion: "... the Internet has achieved, and continues to achieve, the most participatory marketplace of mass speech that this country -- indeed the world -- has yet seen. The plaintiffs in these actions correctly describe the 'democratizing' effects of Internet communication: Individual citizens of limited means can speak to a worldwide audience on issues of concern to them ... The government ... implicitly asks this court to limit both the amount of speech on the Internet and the availability of that speech. This argument is profoundly repugnant to the First Amendment principles."

June 30, 1996 - The Department of Justice, citing a desire to "assist parents in protecting children from sexually explicit material on the Internet," appeals the Dalzell panel's ruling to the Supreme Court.
July 29, 1996 - In its Shea v. Justice Department decision, the U.S. District Court in Brooklyn unanimously rules the CDA unconstitutional.
Aug. 15, 1996 - Department of Justice appeals the decision.
Dec. 7, 1996 - The Supreme Court agrees to hear Reno v. ACLU.
March 19, 1997 - The court hears arguments on Reno v. ACLU, and most of the justices appear skeptical of the government's defense of the law.
June 26, 1997 - Voting 7-2, the court strikes down the Net decency act as an unconstitutional abridgement of the right to freedom of speech.
